title: Generic Total for Any Number Type
oneLiner: Write one Total method that adds up a sequence of ints, longs, decimals or doubles, using generic math in C# and a constrained type variable in Python.
keyTakeaway: where T : INumber<T> lets generic code use + and T.Zero, because static abstract interface members put operators and constants on the type parameter. The same loop then sums ints, longs without overflow, decimals exactly (0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3) and doubles inexactly (0.30000000000000004). Python needs no constraint to run, only to type check.
explanation:
Write Total(items), which returns the sum of a sequence of numbers of any one numeric type, and the type's zero for an empty sequence. Each test calls it five times: on a list of ints; on the same numbers times a billion as longs (an int would overflow); on amounts in cents divided by 100 as decimals; on the same amounts as doubles; and on an empty list of ints. With ints [1, 2, 3] and cents [10, 20] the results are [6, 6000000000, 0.3, 0.30000000000000004, 0]: decimal stores 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, double can't.

In C# the signature is static T Total<T>(IEnumerable<T> items) where T : INumber<T> (System.Numerics is already imported for you). Start from T.Zero, a static member that the constraint makes available on the type parameter, and add with +=, which INumber<T> also promises. Don't convert to double or decimal along the way: each type must be added in its own arithmetic.

In Python the code is a simple loop (or sum), and the typing is the interesting part: def total[T: (int, float, Decimal)](items: Iterable[T]) -> T declares a constrained type variable, so a type checker knows that summing Decimals gives a Decimal. The checker converts your Decimal result to a float to report it.

visualizationSteps.message: T = decimal. The constraint where T : INumber<T> is what makes T.Zero and + available.
Add 0.1: decimal stores base-10 digits, so 0.1 is exact.
The same code with T = double: binary floating point can't store 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, and the error shows.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
from decimal import Decimal


def check_total(ints, cents):
    return [
        total(ints),
        total([i * 1_000_000_000 for i in ints]),
        float(total([Decimal(c) / 100 for c in cents])),
        total([c / 100 for c in cents]),
        total([]),
    ]

complexity.note: One pass with one addition per item; only the running total is kept. Generic math compiles to the same code as a hand-written loop for each number type.

referenceSolutions.python:
from collections.abc import Iterable
from decimal import Decimal


def total[T: (int, float, Decimal)](items: Iterable[T]) -> T:
    result = 0
    for item in items:
        result = result + item
    return result
